newsitem.title: USA: Former communist nations face big task - Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: Former communist nations face big task - Greenspan.

text.p: The transition of former communist countries to capitalism is likely to be slow, painful and halting but the face of the world economy is gradually changing with the rise of free markets, Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said on Tuesday.

"Changing attitudes toward property and profit is not simple," he said in a speech for delivery here to the Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars. "These attitudes derive from the deepest values of personal worth people hold."
The speech makes no mention of current U.S. economic conditions.

In his speech, Greenspan argued that successful economies are rooted in the protection of property, free speech and other rights that limit the influence of the government and allow the markets to have greater sway.
"A list or bill of rights enforced by an impartial judiciary is...the guiding mechanism of a free market economy," Greenspan said.

The widespread dissemination of timely financial and other information is also essential, he said. Otherwise, market players will have to depend on dubious information and rumors, leading to misjudgements and lessening economic efficiency.

"The presumption of property ownership and the legality of its transfer must be deeply embedded in the culture of a society for free market economies to function effectively," the central bank chief added.

Changing cultural attitudes is a long and difficult process, however. "The process of full transition from the so-called collective rights of socialist economies to the individual property rights of market economies and legal certainties can be expected to be slow," he said.
There has already been much pain and periodic backtracking by transition economies, and "there will doubtless be more".

But, he added: "Despite the ebb and flow of governments of differing persuasions, the face of the world economy continues to edge toward free market-oriented societies...as increasing numbers of transition economies prosper and emerging market economies wedded to free market paradigms grow impressively."
Greenspan acknowledged though that not all democracies are the same and noted that Singaporeans do not enjoy some of the rights that their counterparts in the west do.
"There are those who argue, however, that as this remarkable city-state evolves, increasing wealth will push it toward broader freedoms," the Fed chief said.
